citation: (1) Spracklen, Wijewickrama, Sakib, Maiti, Viswanath, Jadliwala. 'We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs'. arXiv:2406.10279, v1 12 Jun 2024, v3 2 Mar 2025; arXiv comments say to appear at USENIX Security 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279. (2) OWASP GenAI Security Project, Agentic Security Initiative (author John Sotiropoulos), 'OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications' (2026 edition), announced 9 Dec 2025. https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/ and https://genai.owasp.org/2025/12/09/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-the-benchmark-for-agentic-security-in-the-age-of-autonomous-ai/. (3) OWASP GenAI Exploit Round-up Q3 2026, 8 Oct 2026. https://genai.owasp.org/2026/10/08/genai-and-agentic-ai-exploit-roundup-q3-2026/
source_tier: Spracklen et al.: preprint, accepted at USENIX Security 2025 (peer-reviewed venue; the acceptance is stated in arXiv comments, not independently confirmed). OWASP Top 10 and Q3 roundup: community-developed practitioner guidance from a nonprofit project, not academic peer review.

date_and_recency: Spracklen: submitted June 2024, revised March 2025; models tested are 2023-era (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, CodeLlama, DeepSeek, etc.), so rates for current models are unknown. OWASP Top 10: 9 Dec 2025. Q3 roundup: 8 Oct 2026, covering incidents May to Aug 2026.
key_claims: Spracklen: code-generating LLMs recommend non-existent packages at a measurable rate, the names repeat, and so they are a viable target for registration by an attacker (package confusion).
Spracklen: tested mitigations (RAG, self-refinement, fine-tuning, ensemble) reduce hallucination, but fine-tuning cost code quality.

OWASP Top 10 names ten agentic risks: ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI08 Cascading Failures, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, ASI10 Rogue Agents.

OWASP: prompt-borne hidden instructions can redirect an agent (ASI01); MCP and A2A runtime components can be poisoned (ASI04); polished agent explanations can lead humans to approve harmful actions (ASI09).

OWASP Q3 2026 roundup: documents an MCP server that changed tool metadata after approval (Deadbugz, disclosed 12 Aug 2026, no confirmed compromise) and malicious repository configuration that executed when a repo was opened in an AI coding tool (Miasma / Mini Shai-Hulud, May to June 2026).
headline_figures: Spracklen Abstract: 576,000 code samples, 16 LLMs, two languages (Python, JavaScript). Average hallucination rate at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models.
Spracklen Sec. 5.1: about 2.23 million packages recommended; 440,445 (19.7%) hallucinated; 205,474 unique non-existent names.
Spracklen Sec. 5.1: GPT-4 Turbo 3.59%, GPT-4 4.05%, GPT-3.5 5.76%; Python average 15.8%, JavaScript 21.3%.
Spracklen Sec. 5.3: across 10 repeated queries, 43% of hallucinated packages recurred in all 10 runs, 39% never recurred.
Spracklen Sec. 5.4: 81% of distinct hallucinated names came from only one model; 0.17% (133) matched previously deleted PyPI packages.
Spracklen Table 4 (DeepSeek / CodeLlama): baseline 16.14% / 26.28%; RAG 12.24% / 13.40%; self-refinement 13.04% / 25.51%; fine-tuning 2.66% / 10.27%; ensemble 2.40% / 9.32%.
Spracklen Table 5: fine-tuned DeepSeek HumanEval pass@1 fell from 51.4% to 25.3%; CodeLlama from 19.6% to 16.4%.
Spracklen Sec. 5.2: GPT-4 hallucinated 8.9% vs 31.8% for GPT-3.5 at maximum temperature.
sample_unit_and_population: Spracklen: LLM-generated code samples (not engineers or incidents); about 9,600 Stack Overflow-derived prompts plus about 9,600 LLM-generated prompts, 2023 'recent' vs pre-2023 'all-time'; 16 models, open-source ones GPTQ-quantized. OWASP Top 10: expert-consensus list from more than 100 contributors, not a measured sample. Q3 roundup: individual disclosed incidents.
observed_vs_stated: Spracklen: observed model output, measured by checking names against package registries. No developer behaviour was observed; the trust assumption in Sec. 3 is an assumption of the threat model. OWASP Top 10: expert judgement and incident-informed, not measured prevalence. Roundup: reported incidents, many with no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.
what_makes_trust_justified: Spracklen: verification of every dependency name against the registry (existence is checkable), plus mitigations that lower but do not remove hallucination (RAG, fine-tuning, ensembles). OWASP Q3 roundup controls: snapshot MCP tool definitions at approval and require re-approval on change; treat adding an MCP server as a controlled dependency change; review agent configuration files as executable supply-chain artifacts; pin dependencies with integrity hashes; require explicit confirmation for sensitive actions; constrain connector scopes and outbound destinations; require human approval before publishing to public infrastructure. Whether a specific model's output can be trusted for a dependency choice is not established by either source for current models.
what_it_costs: Registry and name checks are cheap and automatable. Re-approval of MCP definitions and review of agent config changes add review steps per change. Spracklen's fine-tuning mitigation cost code quality (HumanEval pass@1 halved for DeepSeek). Confirmation prompts add friction and may produce approval fatigue (this last point is my inference, not in the sources) [uncertain].
failure_mode_class: Security: supply chain (slopsquatting, poisoned MCP tools), prompt injection through content the agent reads, malicious repo config executing on open. Also human-agent trust exploitation (ASI09) as an over-reliance route.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Slopsquatting: a dependency allowlist or registry-existence-and-age check before install, with human review of new dependencies. MCP tool poisoning: pin and diff tool metadata, re-approve on change (per the Q3 roundup). Repository-content injection: treat repo content and agent config as untrusted input, review changes to agent configuration, and do not let the agent act on sensitive tools without explicit confirmation. Control mapping to specific incidents is the roundup's wording; the Top 10 PDF mitigations were not read.
limitations_stated: Spracklen: newer models not tested; few commercial models tested due to funding constraints; master package lists may already contain malicious packages so rates are a lower bound; package names cannot be definitively extracted from code so three heuristics were used. Authors did not register hallucinated names, so real-world exploitation was not demonstrated. Roundup: many incidents have no confirmed compromise or in-the-wild exploitation, and it states no repo-content prompt-injection case or confirmed slopsquatting case.
counter_evidence: Spracklen: only 0.17% of hallucinations matched previously deleted packages; 81% of names were unique to one model and 39% never repeated, which limits how easily an attacker can predict a name. The paper is internally inconsistent about prompt recency (Sec. 5.2 says older prompts had 10% higher rates, and also that models hallucinated more on recent topics). Models tested are old relative to Oct 2026; current agents that run installs and check the registry may behave differently [uncertain]. No source here shows a confirmed in-the-wild slopsquatting attack on an agent user. The Q3 roundup item about an agent publishing a malicious replacement package is a different pattern (agent-created, not attacker-registered).

OWASP ten risk names and one-line descriptions: checked against the OWASP announcement page opened. OWASP Top 10 per-item detail, prevention lists and 'least agency' wording: NOT verified, the PDF could not be opened [uncertain]. Q3 roundup incident details: read on the OWASP page, but incident primary sources not opened [uncertain]. The Deadbugz and Miasma entries should not be cited as fact beyond 'OWASP's roundup reports'.
usable_claim: In a 2025 USENIX Security paper, Spracklen and colleagues generated 576,000 code samples from 16 models and found an average package hallucination rate of at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, and that many hallucinated names repeat across runs. Existence of a dependency is cheap to check, so the generated import list needs a check that the output does not provide itself. OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications lists goal hijack through content the agent reads, poisoned MCP components and over-trust in polished agent explanations among its ten risks, which means content the agent reads cannot be treated as trusted instruction.
do_not_use: Do not claim slopsquatting attacks are widespread or have been seen in the wild (not shown by these sources). Do not apply 2023-era model rates to current tools. Do not quote OWASP mitigations or 'least agency' wording from the Top 10 itself (not opened). Do not describe the Deadbugz or Miasma incidents as confirmed compromises or as prompt injection. Do not call the Spracklen paper simply 'peer-reviewed' without noting the arXiv version is a preprint accepted at USENIX Security 2025. Do not cite the 'agent published a malicious package' item as slopsquatting.
